title: Agatha Christie: Queen of the Murder Mystery
summary: Josh Clark and Chuck Bryant profile Agatha Christie, the English crime novelist often cited as the best-selling novelist of all time. They discuss the cozy mystery formula and her detectives Hercule Poirot and Miss Marple, her early life in Torquay, her first published novel The Mysterious Affair at Styles, her 1926 disappearance and the Swan Hydropathic Hotel episode, her second marriage to Max Mallowan and archaeology travels, her theatre success with The Mousetrap, racist and anti-Semitic language in some of her books, and the legacy of And Then There Were None. The episode closes with a listener email from ten-year-old Emmett and a sign-off.
topics: red herrings and bluffs in mysteries

segments.title: Opening banter and Agatha Christie introduction
segments.summary: Hosts banter about Agatha Christie, a book Chuck once had signed by her, and their picks for the episode. They discuss her sales claims and the cozy mystery genre, and mention the film Crooked House.

segments.title: Mystery formula and famous detectives
segments.summary: The hosts describe the formula of classic mystery novels: a murder that is usually off-page, an eccentric detective, a confined setting, suspects with motives, and a final reveal. They name Hercule Poirot and Miss Marple and discuss how Christie's books play fair with readers, including bluffs and red herrings.
topics: red herrings and bluffs in mysteries

segments.title: Christie's early life and first writing
segments.summary: Christie was born in Torquay, Devon, in 1890 and had a solitary, shy childhood raised by governesses. Her family was upper middle class. She began writing at the urging of her sister and later wrote seriously to earn money after marrying Archie Christie. She worked in a pharmacy during World War One, learning about poisons.

segments.title: The Mysterious Affair at Styles and early publishing
segments.summary: Her first published novel, The Mysterious Affair at Styles, introduced Poirot. It was rejected at first and published in 1920 after she agreed to change the ending. Her daughter Rosalind was born in 1919. She published a book a year through the 1920s.

segments.title: The 1926 disappearance
segments.summary: In December 1926, after Archie asked for a divorce, Christie vanished, and her abandoned car was found near a rock quarry. A large search followed. A hotel band later recognized her at the Swan Hydropathic Hotel in Yorkshire, where she had registered under another name. She later cited amnesia, but the hosts describe this as a likely cover story after a suicide attempt.

segments.title: Later life, Max Mallowan, and archaeology
segments.summary: After her divorce she kept her name and traveled to Iraq and Syria. She met archaeologist Max Mallowan and married him, and they stayed together for about forty-six years. She wrote Murder in Mesopotamia, Death on the Nile, and Murder on the Orient Express in the 1930s, which made her an international star. Her Miss Marple debut was Murder at the Vicarage in 1930.

segments.title: Legacy, The Mousetrap, racism in her work, and final detective novels
segments.summary: The Mousetrap ran in London's West End from 1952 and is the longest-running play there. The hosts discuss racist and anti-Semitic language in some of her books and her role in the slasher film genre through And Then There Were None. They describe Curtain and Sleeping Murder, which were published posthumously. She died in 1976 at age 85, and the hosts mention the Murder by Death spoof.

segments.title: Listener mail from Emmett
segments.summary: A ten-year-old listener from Iowa named Emmett writes in about his love of the show and the Atlanta Falcons, and asks for a birthday shout-out. The hosts read his email and wish him a happy birthday.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: The hosts close the episode and give the email address for listener mail.
